title: Round Hill is suing Suno and Anthropic for up to $1B apiece. It isn’t looking to settle.

reading.body:
The core failure here is a data-sourcing decision made before deployment. Suno admitted its model was trained on essentially all music files on the internet, and reporting based on a hack identified YouTube, Deezer, and Genius among the scraped sources. That data collection happened upstream of the product, meaning the legal exposure was baked into the model before any user ever made a request. The failure is not in the generation step alone but in the absence of licensing or rights-clearance at the training stage.

The outputs themselves then demonstrated a second, concrete problem. Record labels showed they could use prompts describing genre, decade, and artist style to repeatedly generate audio closely resembling specific copyrighted recordings, including identifiable versions of well-known songs. That reproducibility suggests the model memorized or closely approximated protected material rather than learning only abstract musical structure. A rights audit of outputs, or filtered training data, would have been the points at which this could have been caught before litigation.

A German court ruled against Suno in a case brought by GEMA, and some record-label suits have reached settlement, including one between Suno and Warner Music Group that also produced a partnership agreement. Class actions from independent artists and suits from music publishers remain active. What is not established is any finding of deliberate intent to infringe, and the settlements reached so far are not admissions of liability.

summary:
Major record labels including Universal Music Group, Sony Music, Warner Music, Atlantic Records, and Capitol Records have sued two popular AI music generators, Udio and Suno, for copyright infringement. The labels claim both companies scraped thousands of copyrighted songs without permission to train their AI models and are now generating music that directly reproduces sections of famous recordings. The lawsuits allege the companies have been deliberately secretive about their training data, though both previously claimed their use of copyrighted material constitutes fair use. The record labels submitted a massive list of scraped works, including music from The Beatles, Frank Sinatra, Bruce Springsteen, Michael Jackson, and many others.

To prove their case, the record labels demonstrated they could repeatedly recreate famous songs by using specific prompts describing musical characteristics like decade, genre, and artist style. Examples include generating songs that replicate Chuck Berry's "Johnny B. Goode," Bill Haley's style, and an almost identical version of Mariah Carey's "All I Want for Christmas Is You." The labels claim this degree of similarity would be impossible if the AI models weren't trained on these copyrighted recordings. The lawsuits were filed in New York and Massachusetts and include unnamed individuals accused of helping scrape the music.
